collection: Primary 4 English reading and writing; phishing delivery forms
note: Twenty-six original English Studies structured tasks and three Basic Digital Literacy structured tasks. Eight original reading stimuli plus four written-production/purpose tasks. All drafts await independent academic review. Written work does not establish oral, aural or digital performance.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.topic: Reading poems, short stories and plays
questions.learningObjective: Read short stories and plays and discuss characters, plots, settings and themes.
questions.prompt: Where does the main action of The Borrowed Sign take place? Give one detail that supports your answer.
questions.answer: At a school preparing for an exhibition, around the courtyard and displays. The library stall, display or school exhibition supports this setting.
questions.explanation: A setting answer must fit the story rather than inventing a different location.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the school exhibition setting.
Uses a relevant detail such as the courtyard, display or library stall.

questions.passage:
The Borrowed Sign
Before the school exhibition, Nnenna borrowed a cardboard sign from the library. A sudden gust bent it while she carried it across the courtyard. She hid it behind her display, afraid that the librarian would refuse to lend her anything again. When visitors began asking where the library stall was, Nnenna brought out the damaged sign and explained what had happened. The librarian fetched tape, and they repaired it together. Nnenna then placed a small stone beside its stand to steady it. She felt relieved: the stall had its sign, and she no longer had to hide the truth.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem in The Wrong Beat? Explain why playing louder does not solve it.
questions.answer: Musa rushes and adds an extra beat, so the group loses time. More volume does not correct the rhythm and makes the confusion worse.
questions.explanation: The conflict concerns timing and listening rather than weak sound.

markingGuide.description: Identifies rushing/adding a beat or losing the shared rhythm.
Explains why loudness does not correct the timing.

questions.passage:
The Wrong Beat
Musa could play the opening drum pattern for the class performance, but he always hurried the last part. At rehearsal he played louder whenever his friends lost their place. That only made everyone more confused. Their teacher asked the group to clap the pattern slowly without drums. Musa noticed that he was adding an extra beat. He practised the difficult part softly until he could keep time with the others. On performance day, he watched the group leader’s hand before beginning. The audience heard one steady rhythm. Musa smiled when he realised that listening had helped more than playing loudly.

questions.prompt: What change has the rain made to the yard in After the Rain? Use the poem in your answer.
questions.answer: It has washed away dust and refreshed the green plants. The ending says the rain washed the dusty yard and brought its green again.
questions.explanation: The answer identifies a change rather than merely stating that rain fell.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the cleaner/refreshed yard.
Supports it with the ending or unfolding leaves.

questions.passage:
After the Rain
The gutter hums a silver song,
The thirsty leaves unfold;
A puddle holds the cloudy sky,
A mirror edged with gold.
My sandals splash the narrow path,
Then rest beside the door;
The rain has washed the dusty yard,
And brought its green once more.

questions.passage:
The Seed Box
A seed slept in my little box,
Too dry to stretch or grow;
I tucked it into soft brown earth
And watered it just so.
A shoot rose like a tiny spear,
Then opened leaves of green;
I checked its pot each morning,
To find what could be seen.

questions.passage:
One More Rehearsal
[In a classroom. Two pupils are preparing a short play.]
ZAINAB: We have time for one more rehearsal before lunch.
EMEKA: Then let us practise the part where I enter. I keep missing your last line.
ZAINAB: I can shout it.
EMEKA: You do not need to shout. Pause after it, and I will listen for the word basket.
[They try the scene. Emeka enters at the right moment.]
ZAINAB: That worked! We should remember the pause.
EMEKA: And I should listen instead of counting the lines on my fingers.

markingGuide.description: Identifies Zainab’s pause.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.topic: Comprehension: main and supporting ideas
questions.learningObjective: Identify main ideas in class-appropriate informational texts.
questions.prompt: State the main idea of The Shared Book Shelf in one sentence.
questions.answer: Careful organisation and simple routines make a shared book shelf work well for its readers.
questions.explanation: The main idea covers several details instead of focusing only on one label or one day.

markingGuide.description: Identifies effective organisation/routines for sharing books.
Connects that organisation to keeping books useful/available for readers.

questions.passage:
The Shared Book Shelf
A class can make a book-sharing shelf useful by organising it carefully. In one fictional school, pupils placed storybooks on the lower shelf and information books above them. A simple label showed where each kind belonged. The class also kept a borrowing card inside each book. A borrower wrote a class code and a return date on the card, so the book could be found when it was needed again. The teacher checked the shelf every Friday and helped repair loose covers. These small routines kept the books available for more readers. A shelf filled with books was helpful, but a clear system made sharing work.

questions.subject: English Studies

questions.learningObjective: Identify main ideas in class-appropriate informational texts.
questions.prompt: What is the main message of Choosing Books to Give?
questions.answer: A useful book donation should be chosen and checked to match the readers’ needs, rather than judged only by its size.
questions.explanation: The final sentence brings together asking, selecting, checking and listing.

markingGuide.description: Identifies matching the recipients’ needs.
Includes careful selection/checking rather than quantity alone.

questions.passage:
Choosing Books to Give
A class wanted to donate books to a small reading club. Before collecting anything, the pupils asked the club organiser which books would be useful. The organiser requested short stories with clear print. The pupils sorted the donations, separating books with complete pages from those with missing endings. They set aside damaged copies for repair instead of putting them straight into the gift box. They also made a short list of the titles. This helped the organiser plan reading sessions. A thoughtful donation was not simply the heaviest box: it was a collection that matched the readers’ needs.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.topic: Informal Letters
questions.learningObjective: Write informal letters.
questions.prompt: Write an informal letter to a fictional cousin about a class reading corner. Describe what pupils can find there, explain one activity you enjoyed and invite your cousin to tell you about reading at their school. Include a fictional sender’s address, date, greeting, friendly body, closing and name/signature. Do not use your real address.
questions.answer:
14 Lantern Close,
Example Town.
19 November 2026.
Dear Femi,
How are you? We have made a reading corner beside our classroom window. It has storybooks, poems and a mat where we can sit comfortably.
Yesterday I read a funny play with two classmates. We changed our voices for the different characters, and everyone laughed at the ending.
What do you enjoy reading at your school? Please write and tell me.
Your cousin,
Sade
Sade (signature)
questions.explanation: Accept varied original letters that fulfil the purpose. This is original practice, with no official word limit or national mark scheme claimed. Handwriting or a prepared word processor may be used; digital saving is not assessed.

markingGuide.description: Includes a fictional address, suitable date and personal greeting.
Describes the reading corner clearly.
Develops an enjoyed activity and invites a reply about the cousin’s reading.
Uses a friendly organised body with understandable sentences.
Includes a suitable closing and sender’s name/signature.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.topic: Narrative and Descriptive Composition
questions.learningObjective: Write a narrative composition.
questions.prompt: Write a short narrative called The Day Our Display Fell Over. You may invent the event. Introduce the people and place, tell events in a clear order, explain how the problem was handled and give an ending.
questions.answer:
We were arranging our class display before the visitors arrived. I stood paper models on a table while Amina fixed the labels. When I lifted a large sheet, it caught one model and knocked the others down.
For a moment, we stared at the floor. Then Amina brought a tray, and we collected the pieces. We rebuilt the smallest models first and moved the display away from the loose sheet.
Our display was simpler than we had planned, but it was ready on time. I felt proud that we had worked together instead of arguing.
questions.explanation: The model is one possible narrative; assess development and sequence rather than matching its wording. No actual personal experience or official word limit is required.

markingGuide.description: Establishes people and setting.
Develops the falling-display problem and a response.
Orders the events clearly with a suitable ending.
Uses understandable linked sentences and suitable narrative tense.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.topic: Narrative and Descriptive Composition
questions.learningObjective: Write a descriptive composition.
questions.prompt: Describe a quiet corner of an imagined school library. Help a reader picture its position, furniture, light and sounds. Keep the focus on describing the place rather than telling a long sequence of events.
questions.answer:
The quiet corner is beside a wide window at the back of the library. Two low wooden chairs face a small round table. A blue cushion rests on each chair, and a basket of picture books stands underneath the table.
Morning light falls across the clean floor. From this corner, I can hear the soft turn of pages and the faint rustle of leaves outside. A little sign asks readers to speak gently. The corner feels calm and welcoming.
questions.explanation: Accept varied coherent descriptions. The place may be invented; assess useful detail and organisation, not claims about a real school.

markingGuide.description: Creates a clear overall picture and position.
Develops specific details of furniture/light.
Includes relevant sounds or another sensory detail.
Organises understandable sentences while maintaining a descriptive focus.

questions.subject: English Studies
questions.topic: Narrative and Descriptive Composition
questions.learningObjective: Differentiate between narrative and descriptive compositions.
questions.prompt: A writer wants to tell how a lost library book was found. Another wants to help readers picture the library building. Which purpose mainly calls for narrative writing, and which mainly calls for descriptive writing? Explain one difference.
questions.answer: Finding the lost book mainly calls for a narrative because it follows events. Picturing the building mainly calls for description because it develops details of a place.
questions.explanation: Narratives may include description, and descriptions may mention actions. The distinction is the main purpose rather than an absolute ban on either feature.

markingGuide.description: Matches the search/finding event to narrative.
Matches the building picture to description.
Explains events versus developed details without treating them as entirely separate ingredients.

questions.answer: Email phishing, text-message phishing and voice-call phishing.

questions.answer: A: email phishing; B: text-message phishing; C: voice-call phishing.

markingGuide.description: Matches A to email.

questions.subject: Basic Digital Literacy
questions.topic: Phishing

questions.prompt: A fictional phishing attempt arrives as an email. Its subject line says Telephone Help, but all of the request is written in the email. Under the lesson’s delivery grouping, is it email phishing or voice-call phishing? Explain.
questions.answer: It is email phishing because it is delivered as a written email; mentioning a telephone in the subject does not make it a voice call.
questions.explanation: The channel is how the attempt actually reaches the reader, not a word in its title. Other grouping systems may describe targeting or techniques instead.

markingGuide.description: Selects email phishing.
Uses the actual delivery channel rather than the subject-line wording.
